author: Augustine of Hippo
note: The famous opening of the Confessions — the restless heart made for God. DELICACY/ACCURACY: the popular English form 'Thou hast made us for Thyself, and our heart is restless until it rests (repose) in Thee' is a paraphrase (and close to Pusey's 1838 wording); the actual NPNF1 Pilkington text reads 'Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee' — quoted verbatim here. Canonical CCEL locus: NPNF1-01 (npnf101), Confessions Bk I ch. 1; verbatim captured from the parallel static NPNF Pilkington page on Wikisource (CCEL leaf pages are JS-rendered and could not be read verbatim by the fetch tool). Em-dash/comma punctuation around 'resistest the proud' to be confirmed at verification. verified verbatim against the NPNF text (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is Thy power, and of Thy wisdom there is no end. And man, being a part of Thy creation, desires to praise Thee, man, who bears about with him his mortality, the witness of his sin, even the witness that Thou 'resistest the proud,'—yet man, this part of Thy creation, desires to praise Thee. Thou movest us to delight in praising Thee; for Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee.

author: Augustine of Hippo
note: The 'Too late loved I Thee' passage — the soul's discovery that God was within all along. ACCURACY: the widely quoted 'O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new' is PUSEY's rendering, NOT this NPNF text; the NPNF1 Pilkington translation reads 'O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new' (Latin: 'pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova') — quoted verbatim here. Canonical CCEL locus: NPNF1-01 (npnf101), Confessions Bk X ch. 27; verbatim captured from the parallel static NPNF Pilkington page on Wikisource (CCEL leaf pages are JS-rendered). verified verbatim (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: Too late did I love Thee, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love Thee! For behold, Thou wert within, and I without, and there did I seek Thee; I, unlovely, rushed heedlessly among the things of beauty Thou madest. Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee. Those things kept me far from Thee, which, unless they were in Thee, were not. Thou calledst, and criedst aloud, and forcedst open my deafness. Thou didst gleam and shine, and chase away my blindness. Thou didst exhale odours, and I drew in my breath and do pant after Thee. I tasted, and do hunger and thirst. Thou didst touch me, and I burned for Thy peace.

author: Augustine of Hippo
translation: Arthur West Haddan, rev. William G. T. Shedd (NPNF ser. 1 vol. 3, 1887), public domain
note: Augustine's summary of the faith of the Trinity he sets out to defend: one substance, indivisible equality, one God, the persons distinct (the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit is the Spirit of both), the Holy Spirit "co-equal with the Father and the Son." An excerpt from the long sentence of 1.7, which begins "...have purposed to teach, according to the Scriptures, this doctrine, that". Chapter 4 of Book 1 in the editors' chapters, so also cited as 1.4.7. Verified word for word against the hosted 1887 text (fathers/), itself checked against three archive.org scans of the 1887 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1887 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit intimate a divine unity of one and the same substance in an indivisible equality; and therefore that they are not three Gods, but one God: although the Father hath begotten the Son, and so He who is the Father is not the Son; and the Son is begotten by the Father, and so He who is the Son is not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, Himself also co-equal with the Father and the Son, and pertaining to the unity of the Trinity.

author: Augustine of Hippo
note: The thesis of The City of God — the two cities distinguished not by geography but by two loves: love of self to the contempt of God (earthly city) versus love of God to the contempt of self (heavenly city). About the orientation of the heart, not double predestination — no reprobation language in the excerpt, so denominationally neutral. Excerpt is the opening of ch. 28 (first three sentences), each verbatim-confirmed from the static NPNF Dods page on Wikisource. Canonical CCEL locus: NPNF1-02 (npnf102). verified verbatim (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self. The former, in a word, glories in itself, the latter in the Lord. For the one seeks glory from men; but the greatest glory of the other is God, the witness of conscience.

author: Augustine of Hippo
note: The closing of The City of God — the eternal Sabbath 'consecrated by the resurrection of Christ,' the repose 'not only of the spirit, but also of the body' (bodily resurrection hope), ending in the beloved line 'There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise.' Both sentences verbatim-confirmed from the static NPNF Dods page on Wikisource. Canonical CCEL locus: NPNF1-02 (npnf102). verified verbatim (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: But there is not now space to treat of these ages; suffice it to say that the seventh shall be our Sabbath, which shall be brought to a close, not by an evening, but by the Lord's day, as an eighth and eternal day, consecrated by the resurrection of Christ, and prefiguring the eternal repose not only of the spirit, but also of the body. There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise. This is what shall be in the end without end.

author: Augustine of Hippo
work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
note: Augustine's 'crede ut intelligas' — 'believe that thou mayest understand.' In §6 this line is introduced by 'For understanding is the reward of faith' (context, not quoted here) and grounded on Isaiah 7:9 LXX ('except ye believe, ye shall not understand'). The load-bearing apologetics locus for 'faith seeking understanding' (later Anselm's 'fides quaerens intellectum'). Sentence verbatim-confirmed from the static NPNF Gibb page on Wikisource (page confirmed as 'Tractate XXIX. Chapter VII. 14-18'). Canonical CCEL locus: NPNF1-07 (npnf107). NOTE: this is NPNF vol. 7, outside the vols 1-3 the brief named, but within the task's allowance for a PD NPNF tractate. verified verbatim (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that thou mayest understand; since, 'except ye believe, ye shall not understand.'

author: Augustine of Hippo
translation: Arthur West Haddan, rev. William G. T. Shedd (NPNF ser. 1 vol. 3, 1887), public domain
note: Augustine's rule for the texts that call the Son less than the Father (John 14:28): they speak of him in the form of a servant he took, without losing the form of God in which he is equal to the Father (Phil. 2:6-7). Also cited as 1.7.14. Verified word for word against the hosted 1887 text (fathers/), itself checked against three archive.org scans of the 1887 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1887 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: They say, for instance, that the Son is less than the Father, because it is written that the Lord Himself said, "My Father is greater than I." But the truth shows that after the same sense the Son is less also than Himself; for how was He not made less also than Himself, who "emptied Himself, and took upon Him the form of a servant?" For He did not so take the form of a servant as that He should lose the form of God, in which He was equal to the Father. If, then, the form of a servant was so taken that the form of God was not lost, since both in the form of a servant and in the form of God He Himself is the same only-begotten Son of God the Father, in the form of God equal to the Father, in the form of a servant the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; is there any one who cannot perceive that He Himself in the form of God is also greater than Himself, but yet likewise in the form of a servant less than Himself?

author: Augustine of Hippo
translation: Arthur West Haddan, rev. William G. T. Shedd (NPNF ser. 1 vol. 3, 1887), public domain
note: The Father and the Son are distinguished by relation, not by substance; and the relation is not an accident, because it does not change. Also cited as 5.5.6. Verified word for word against the hosted 1887 text (fathers/), itself checked against three archive.org scans of the 1887 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1887 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: Wherefore, although to be the Father and to be the Son is different, yet their substance is not different; because they are so called, not according to substance, but according to relation, which relation, however, is not accident, because it is not changeable.

author: Augustine of Hippo
translation: Arthur West Haddan, rev. William G. T. Shedd (NPNF ser. 1 vol. 3, 1887), public domain
note: Why Latin-speaking Christians answer "three persons" (Greek writers said three hypostaseis): the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly three, against the Sabellians, yet human language cannot say fully what the three are. The square brackets are the translators'. Also cited as 5.9.10. Verified word for word against the hosted 1887 text (fathers/), itself checked against three archive.org scans of the 1887 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1887 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: For, in truth, as the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father, and that Holy Spirit who is also called the gift of God is neither the Father nor the Son, certainly they are three. And so it is said plurally, "I and my Father are one." For He has not said, "is one," as the Sabellians say; but, "are one." Yet, when the question is asked, What three? human language labors altogether under great poverty of speech. The answer, however, is given, three "persons," not that it might be [completely] spoken, but that it might not be left [wholly] unspoken.

author: Augustine of Hippo
translation: Arthur West Haddan, rev. William G. T. Shedd (NPNF ser. 1 vol. 3, 1887), public domain
note: The limit Augustine sets on his own analogy from the human mind (memory, understanding and love): the image in a man is one person, while the Trinity is three persons, and yet more indivisible. Two sentences of 15.43; the ellipsis marks the text between them. Also cited as 15.23.43. Verified word for word against the hosted 1887 text (fathers/), itself checked against three archive.org scans of the 1887 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1887 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: Nor, again, as that image in the case of man has these three things but is one person, so is it with the Trinity; but therein are three persons, the Father of the Son, and the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of both Father and Son. … A thing certainly wonderfully ineffable, or ineffably wonderful, that while this image of the Trinity is one person, but the Highest Trinity itself is three persons, yet that Trinity of three persons is more indivisible than this of one.

author: Augustine of Hippo
translation: Arthur West Haddan, rev. William G. T. Shedd (NPNF ser. 1 vol. 3, 1887), public domain
note: The prayer that closes On the Trinity: Augustine sets the baptismal command (Matt. 28:19) beside the Shema (Deut. 6:4) and confesses the one Lord God as a Trinity. His argument is from the two texts together, not from the Hebrew word for "one." Also cited as 15.28.51. Verified word for word against the hosted 1887 text (fathers/), itself checked against three archive.org scans of the 1887 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1887 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: O Lord our God, we believe in Thee, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the Truth would not say, Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, unless Thou wast a Trinity. Nor wouldest thou, O Lord God, bid us to be baptized in the name of Him who is not the Lord God. Nor would the divine voice have said, Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God, unless Thou wert so a Trinity as to be one Lord God.
